blocks.text: By sending a tip, you confirm and accept the following.
What you send is information you lawfully have. You did not break into a system or take files you were never given access to.
You are not sending classified national-security information, another person’s medical records, or anything involving a child.
Granite State Report may use what you send for reporting, will try to verify it, and decides on its own whether and how to publish.

Granite State Report does not pay for tips, is not your lawyer, and gives no legal advice. If your job or safety is at stake, talk to a lawyer first. For free civil legal help, call 603 Legal Aid at 1-800-639-5290 or apply at 603legalaid.org.

forms.title: Inside the Building
forms.dek: For the people who work in New Hampshire government and have seen something the public should know.
forms.mainLabel: What happened, and what should the public know? Type it, paste it, or skip it if your files say it.
forms.consent: By sending, you confirm you have read this page, accept the terms above, and are not sending classified information.

blocks.text: The biggest risk to a source is the trail they leave before the reporter ever sees anything. Most people who are identified are identified by their own employer’s systems.
Never use anything your employer owns or runs. No work computer, work phone, work email, work Wi-Fi, or VPN. Your employer can log what crosses them, and work email can itself be a public record.
Do not print, scan, or download at work if you can avoid it. Printers, copiers, and document systems keep logs of who did what and when.
Think about who else saw it. If only three people had a document, sending it narrows the field to three.

Files carry hidden data: author names, edit history, the device that made them, and in photos, often the location. Send a photo of a printout or a screenshot instead of the original file when you can.
Do not tell coworkers. Including the ones you trust.
A story can wait. Your job and your safety come first.

readFirst.heading: What the law says about you speaking up

blocks.text: New Hampshire gives public employees more room to speak than many people realize, and it also sets limits. This is a summary of what the statutes say, not legal advice. If your job is on the line, talk to a lawyer before you act.

RSA 98-E, Public Employee Freedom of Expression. Anyone employed by the state or any subdivision of it, including counties, cities, towns, school districts, and school administrative units, has “a full right to publicly discuss and give opinions as an individual on all matters concerning any government entity and its policies.” The law says no person shall interfere with a public employee’s freedom of speech, full criticism, or disclosure, and it lets an employee go to court for damages and attorney’s fees if someone does. The limit: RSA 98-E:3 says the chapter does not change any law on confidential or privileged records, and it names law-enforcement investigation records and collective bargaining proceedings. Speaking about what your agency is doing is one thing. Handing over records the law makes confidential is another.

RSA 275-E, the Whistleblowers’ Protection Act. It covers government employers. It protects an employee who, in good faith, reports what they reasonably believe is a violation of law, refuses to take part in what they believe is illegal, or takes part in a government investigation or hearing. It does not mention reporters. Before a hearing with the labor commissioner, RSA 275-E:4 expects the employee to have first used any grievance process at work.

Federal employees. Under 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8), a federal agency cannot retaliate against an employee for disclosing what they reasonably believe shows a violation of law, gross mismanagement, gross waste, abuse of authority, or a substantial and specific danger to public health or safety, as long as the disclosure is not specifically prohibited by law and the information is not required by executive order to be kept secret for national defense or foreign affairs. Several intelligence agencies, including the FBI, CIA, and NSA, are outside that section. Classified information has its own channels: the Office of Special Counsel, an agency Inspector General, or Congress. A newsroom is not one of them. Do not send classified material here. It will not be used.

readFirst.heading: What Granite State Report promises, and what it cannot

blocks.text: Your name stays out. Granite State Report will not publish your name or anything that points to you unless you say in writing that it can.

GSR will refuse any demand to identify you, and will fight it. The New Hampshire Supreme Court recognized a reporter’s privilege to protect confidential sources in State v. Siel, 122 N.H. 254 (1982), under the state constitution and the First Amendment.

No newsroom can promise more than the law allows. That privilege is qualified. A judge can order disclosure when the party asking meets a strict test. The best protection is information GSR never had, so share only what is needed to check the story.
What you send is checked. Nothing is published on one person’s word. Documents are verified, and the agency is asked to respond, as the Code of Ethics requires.
Want terms before you send anything? Call or write first and ask. A promise made to a source is kept.
By sending anything through this page, you confirm and accept the following.
You are sending information you lawfully have. You did not break into a system, take files you were never given access to, or go somewhere you were not allowed to be.
You are not sending classified national-security information, another person’s medical records, or anything involving a child.
Granite State Report may use what you send for reporting, will try to verify it, and decides on its own whether and how to publish. Sending something does not guarantee a story.
Granite State Report does not pay for information and does not act as your lawyer or advocate. Nothing on this page is legal advice.
Granite State Report will protect your identity as described above. You may ask at any time how your information is being handled.

readFirst.heading: Read this before you send anything

blocks.text: This form is not anonymous. It is convenient, and convenient is not the same as safe.

The site is hosted by WordPress.com (Automattic). Files you send are stored on this site’s server there, the entry is kept in the site’s private Drop Box, and a notice is emailed to the newsroom’s Gmail account and to the editor’s personal Gmail account. Files are encrypted as they arrive, and the notice gives counts and sizes only: no files, no file names, nothing you typed.
Like every page load, sending this form leaves your IP address, browser, and the time with the hosting platform, as the Privacy Policy describes.
Files carry hidden data: author names, the computer or phone that made them, edit history, and in photos, often the location. Printed pages can carry printer tracking marks.
Never use a work computer, a work phone, or a work network. Your employer can see what crosses them. A call or a text from your own phone leaves a record with your carrier.
If being identified could cost you a job, your safety, or your freedom, use the mail, or wait. A document will keep. You cannot take back a trail.

readFirst.heading: Send what you have a right to have

blocks.text: Do not break into anything, take a file from a place you were not allowed to be, or copy what you were never given access to. If the only way to get a document is to take it, do not. Tell this newsroom where it is instead, using the box marked Can’t send it? Every person in New Hampshire has the same right to ask for public records under RSA 91-A, and asking for the right record by name is often all it takes.

If your job is on the line, talk to a lawyer first. New Hampshire’s Whistleblowers’ Protection Act, RSA 275-E:2, is written around reporting a violation of law and taking part in a government investigation. It says nothing about talking to a reporter. Granite State Report is a newsroom, not a law firm, and nothing on this page is legal advice.

topSections.heading: Animal hurt, someone in danger, or a crime?

blocks.text: People in danger: call 911.
A wildlife emergency or a wildlife crime in progress: New Hampshire Fish and Game dispatch, (603) 271-3361, 24 hours a day.
Poaching or another wildlife law violation: Operation Game Thief, 1-800-344-4262, 24 hours a day.
An orphaned deer, moose, or bear: Fish and Game, (603) 271-3361. For other young animals that look orphaned, and for bear questions, the Wildlife Division: (603) 271-2461 or wildlife@wildlife.nh.gov.
An injured animal: only people with a rehabilitator permit from Fish and Game may take in and care for injured or orphaned wildlife. The department keeps a list of licensed rehabilitators.
A bear in the birdfeeder or the chickens: USDA Wildlife Services, (603) 223-6832, the number Fish and Game lists for wildlife conflicts.
Then send GSR the footage.

New Hampshire Fish and Game says it has never received verifiable evidence, photographic or DNA, of mountain lions living in the state. Reports that came with photographs, it says, have been misidentified bobcats or house cats, or mountain lion pictures taken from the internet. That is the kind of question a good photo settles. Granite State Report wants the bear in the yard, the moose in the road, the animal acting strangely, and the one nobody can name, and it checks each one before it runs.
The original file, straight from your phone, camera, or trail camera. Not a screenshot or a copy saved from social media. The original can carry the date, the time, and the place.
When and where: the date, the time, the town, and the spot.
What you think it is, and about how far away it was.
Anything unusual: an animal that looked sick, hurt, tagged, collared, or out of place.

If the species is on its list, report it to NH Wildlife Sightings too; the list centers on the species the state’s Wildlife Action Plan names as in greatest conservation need. That project is a joint effort of Fish and Game, the University of New Hampshire, the NH Natural Heritage Bureau, and NH Audubon, and it uses photos so wildlife professionals can confirm what the animal is.
By sending, you confirm and accept the following.
You took the photo or video yourself, or you have the right to send it.

You keep your copyright. Granite State Report may review what you send, show it to experts asked to help check it, and, if it becomes part of a story, publish it with the credit you choose under “Add details” in the box below: your name, or no name at all.
Granite State Report decides whether and how to publish, publishes nothing on one person’s word, and does not pay for footage.

Faces of people who did not agree to be shown, and anything that identifies a child, are blurred or cut before anything runs. If the exact spot you filmed from is private, say so in your note and it stays out.
How your name and contact details are handled, and the legal limits of what any newsroom can promise, are on Send a Tip.

Moose. Fish and Game’s warning: “Moose are bigger and faster than any person and give little warning before attacking a perceived threat.” The department says no one should ever approach them, however calm they seem.

Bears. “If you see a bear, keep your distance,” the department says. New Hampshire sets no distance in feet. Yellowstone National Park, for comparison, requires visitors to stay at least 100 yards from bears. A long lens beats a short walk.

Never feed or bait an animal for a picture. Fish and Game says it is illegal to intentionally feed bears in New Hampshire. Under its rule, Fis 310.01, a person told by the department to stop putting out what draws bears can be fined for not doing it.

Stay where you are allowed to be. Under New Hampshire’s criminal trespass law, a person is guilty if, “knowing that he is not licensed or privileged to do so, he enters or remains in any place” (RSA 635:2, I). No clip is worth a charge.

Drones. Recreational flyers must pass the FAA’s free online safety test, known as TRUST, and carry proof of it. They must stay at or below 400 feet in uncontrolled airspace and need FAA authorization, through LAANC or DroneZone, to fly in controlled airspace near airports (FAA, Recreational Flyers).
Time and place, from the original file and your note.
The animal: what it is, checked with wildlife biologists and, where it matters, Fish and Game.
The picture: a reverse image search, because a photo that has run somewhere before is not a new sighting.
People: neighbors, other witnesses, other cameras on the same road.
Every submission ends one of three ways. Confirmed, and GSR says what it shows. Not what it looked like, and GSR says what it was. Not enough to go on, and nothing runs.
More from GSR on wildlife: Coyotes in NH: A Guide to Understanding Our Wild Neighbors.

blocks.text: The original file, straight from your phone or camera. Not a screenshot, a screen recording, or a copy saved from social media. The original can carry the date, the time, and the place your device recorded.
When: the date and the clock time.
Where: the town, the spot, and which way you were facing.
What it did: how long it lasted, how it moved, and whether it made a sound.
Who else saw it. A second witness or a second camera angle is worth more than a sharper picture.
Paranormal footage gets the same treatment: the original file, the place, the time, and anyone else who was there.

readFirst.heading: Check it yourself first, if you like

blocks.text: A line of lights moving together is probably a train of Starlink satellites, and the National UFO Reporting Center asks people not to report those. Heavens-Above predicts satellite passes, Starlink included, for any location, and can run the predictions for past dates.

A very bright, silver-white light that sits still near the horizon is likely Venus, the reporting center says. Stellarium is free, open-source planetarium software that shows the sky for any date, time, and place.
Aircraft that broadcast their position show up on ADS-B Exchange, which does not filter out military flights that are broadcasting and has a replay feature for past times.
Something in the video that you did not see with your own eyes is probably the camera, the reporting center says.
Still doesn’t fit? Send it anyway. A list of what you ruled out helps.
By sending, you confirm and accept the following.
You took the photo or video yourself, or you have the right to send it.

You keep your copyright. Granite State Report may review what you send, show it to experts asked to help check it, and, if it becomes part of a story, publish it with the credit you choose under “Add details” in the box below: your name, or no name at all.
Granite State Report decides whether and how to publish, publishes nothing on one person’s word, and does not pay for footage.

Faces of people who did not agree to be shown, and anything that identifies a child, are blurred or cut before anything runs. If the exact spot you filmed from is private, say so in your note and it stays out.
How your name and contact details are handled, and the legal limits of what any newsroom can promise, are on Send a Tip.

Stay where you are allowed to be. Under New Hampshire’s criminal trespass law, a person is guilty if, “knowing that he is not licensed or privileged to do so, he enters or remains in any place” (RSA 635:2, I). No clip is worth a charge.

Drones. Recreational flyers must pass the FAA’s free online safety test, known as TRUST, and carry proof of it. They must stay at or below 400 feet in uncontrolled airspace and need FAA authorization, through LAANC or DroneZone, to fly in controlled airspace near airports (FAA, Recreational Flyers).

Voices on the recording. New Hampshire’s wiretap law, RSA 570-A, makes it a crime, with exceptions, to record a conversation without the consent of everyone in it when the speakers reasonably expect it is not being recorded. Sky footage rarely raises that. A camera indoors can. GSR’s guide: The Law That Decides When You Can Press Record in New Hampshire.

blocks.text: Never film while driving. Pull over first, or let a passenger do it.
Time and place, from the original file and your note.
The sky that night: aircraft broadcasts, satellite passes, planets and bright stars, and weather balloons, which the National Weather Service sends up from 92 stations, normally twice a day.
People: other witnesses, police logs, nearby airports.
The camera: zoom, focus, reflections in glass, lens flare, compression, and edits.
Experts: astronomers and pilots, and for anything on the ground, people who know the place.
Every report ends one of three ways. Explained, and GSR says what it was. Unexplained after checking, and GSR publishes what was ruled out. Not enough to go on, and nothing runs.
The National UFO Reporting Center takes reports from the public through its online form. Its hotline, 206-722-3000, is for recent sightings only.

The Pentagon’s All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office takes reports only from current or former federal employees, service members, and contractors with direct knowledge of government programs. It says it will announce when the public can report (AARO, Submit a Report).
Pilots: the office encourages civilian pilots to report sightings promptly to air traffic control.
Anyone in danger: call 911.

forms.mainLabel: What is it, and why does it matter? Type it, paste it, or skip it.
forms.sendLabel: Send it to Granite State Report
forms.consent: Not sure it is redacted? Send it anyway. GSR removes private information before anything is published.

blocks.text: New Hampshire keeps its records in ten thousand filing cabinets, and most of them never see daylight. If you have one, this is where it can live: a police report, a town or city record, a state agency letter, a court filing, correspondence with a public office, a response to your own Right-to-Know request. Anything a government body produced or sent you.
Drop the document in the box below, or paste it. Any file type, up to 2 GB each and 50 at a time. Nothing has to be typed, though a line on where it came from helps.
It gets read. Every submission is opened and read by the editor. Nothing is posted automatically.
Provenance gets checked. A record goes into the index only once it is clear what it is, which office produced it, and how it reached you. If that cannot be established, it stays out.

Private information comes out. Names of minors, Social Security and account numbers, dates of birth, home addresses of private people, and medical details are removed before anything is published, whether or not you removed them first.
Then it is public, free, on the same terms as every other item on this page. If it becomes part of a Granite State Report article, the entry above will say so and link to the piece.

Anything you send is treated as on the record unless you say otherwise in the message. This form is not anonymous. What you send is stored on this site’s server with the host, WordPress.com, and a notice is emailed to the newsroom’s Gmail account and to the editor’s personal Gmail account. Files are encrypted as they arrive, and the notice gives counts and sizes only: no files, no file names, nothing you typed. If you need to talk before you send, write to granitestatereport@gmail.com or call (603) 931-9264.
